params.prompt: Rosa wants a health savings account. The law says she may have one only if she is covered by a high-deductible health plan and by no other disqualifying coverage. For two thousand twenty-six an H D H P must have a deductible of at least one thousand seven hundred dollars for self-only coverage or three thousand four hundred dollars for family coverage, and its out-of-pocket maximum may not exceed eight thousand five hundred dollars self-only or seventeen thousand dollars family. The plan may cover preventive care before the deductible. These numbers are indexed each year, so learn the structure and check the current figures before advising a client.

To contribute to an H S A, Rosa must be covered by an H D H P on the first day of the month, must not have other first-dollar medical coverage such as a spouse’s traditional plan or a general purpose flexible spending account, must not be enrolled in Medicare, and must not be claimed as a dependent on someone else’s tax return. Permitted other coverage includes dental, vision, disability, long-term care and specific-disease policies. Dennis, who enrolls in Medicare at sixty-five, must stop contributing, although he may keep spending what he saved. The account belongs to the individual, not the employer.

For two thousand twenty-six the annual H S A contribution limit is four thousand four hundred dollars for self-only coverage and eight thousand seven hundred fifty dollars for family coverage, from all sources combined, with an additional one thousand dollars for account holders age fifty-five or older. Contributions are deductible, or excluded from income when made through payroll. Earnings grow tax-free. Withdrawals for qualified medical expenses, including deductibles, coinsurance, prescriptions, dental and vision care, are tax-free. Withdrawals for anything else are taxed as income plus a twenty percent penalty, which disappears after age sixty-five, death or disability. Unused balances roll over forever and move with the account holder.

An H R A is different in kind. Only the employer funds it; employees may not contribute. The employer owns the account and sets what it reimburses, typically deductibles, coinsurance and other medical expenses, and whether unused amounts carry over. Reimbursements are tax-free to the employee. An H R A need not be paired with an H D H P. Unlike an H S A, it usually does not travel with an employee who leaves. Newer variants let employers reimburse individual market premiums: the individual coverage H R A for any employer and the qualified small employer H R A for employers with fewer than fifty employees that offer no group plan.

Put them side by side. The H S A is the individual’s account: funded by employee, employer or both; requires an H D H P; capped by the annual limit; portable; invested; subject to the twenty percent penalty on nonmedical use. The H R A is the employer’s promise: funded only by the employer; pairs with any plan; limited only by the employer’s design, except the Q S E H R A cap; stays with the employer; no investment account; no nonmedical withdrawals at all. Priya might offer an H D H P with H S A contributions to her bakery staff, or keep a traditional plan and add an H R A to soften its deductible.

Rosa, self-employed and healthy, buys a two thousand twenty-six H D H P with a three thousand dollar deductible and opens an H S A. She may contribute up to four thousand four hundred dollars, deduct it, and pay her deductible from the account tax-free; what she does not spend keeps growing for retirement medical costs. Priya, employing twenty people, compares an H D H P with a one thousand five hundred dollar employer H S A contribution against a traditional plan with a two thousand dollar H R A. Both lower the employees’ exposure; only the H S A money belongs to the employees permanently. Lesson fifty-seven adds flexible spending accounts and the tax rules that tie these accounts together.

Marcus’s older daughter is twenty-four, finished with school, working part time and living in another city. Under the Affordable Care Act she may stay on his plan until she turns twenty-six, regardless of whether she is a student, married, financially dependent or living at home. Maryland law separately requires coverage of unmarried child dependents to age twenty-five; the federal rule governs plans subject to it, and the more generous rule applies. When she reaches twenty-six she loses eligibility, which is a qualifying event for COBRA or Maryland continuation and a special enrollment opportunity on Maryland Health Connection.

Non-grandfathered plans must cover recommended preventive services with no deductible, copayment or coinsurance when delivered in network: screenings and counseling rated A or B by the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force, recommended immunizations, and the preventive care guidelines for women and children. Elena’s mammogram and the children’s vaccines cost nothing out of pocket. Plans may not deny coverage, exclude a condition or charge more because of a pre-existing condition, for adults or children. The HIPAA exclusion periods you learned in Lesson twenty-four are gone from comprehensive coverage.

Before the A C A, some insurers canceled coverage retroactively when a member got sick, hunting the application for errors. Rescission is now permitted only for fraud or an intentional misrepresentation of a material fact, and the insurer must give thirty days’ advance notice so the member can appeal. Honest mistakes cannot cost coverage. Plans also may not impose lifetime dollar limits on essential health benefits, or annual dollar limits on them. A plan may still limit non-essential benefits and may use visit limits that are not dollar caps where permitted. The result is that catastrophic illness no longer exhausts a policy.

A plan that existed on March twenty-three, two thousand ten and has not made significant changes, such as cutting benefits, raising coinsurance, or sharply increasing deductibles or employee contributions, is grandfathered. Grandfathered plans must still cover children to twenty-six, drop lifetime limits and stop rescissions, but they are exempt from some rules: free preventive care, essential health benefits, the new appeals process and the rating limits. Each year fewer remain. Once a plan loses grandfathered status it cannot regain it. Marcus’s employer plan lost its status when it doubled the deductible, so it now meets every A C A rule.

Individual and small group plans must cover ten categories of essential health benefits. Ambulatory patient services. Emergency services. Hospitalization. Maternity and newborn care. Mental health and substance use disorder services, including behavioral health treatment. Prescription drugs. Rehabilitative and habilitative services and devices. Laboratory services. Preventive and wellness services and chronic disease management. Pediatric services, including oral and vision care. Each state picks a benchmark plan that defines the details; Maryland’s benchmark folds in the state mandates. Large group plans are not required to cover all ten but may not put dollar limits on any they do cover.

Run Marcus’s family through the rules. The twenty-four-year-old stays on the plan. Preventive visits are free in network. The younger child’s asthma cannot be excluded or surcharged. If Marcus forgot to list a decade-old prescription on an application, the plan cannot rescind for an honest omission. A four hundred thousand dollar hospital bill cannot exhaust a lifetime maximum, because there is none on essential benefits. And because his employer’s plan is no longer grandfathered, every one of these protections applies. Lesson twenty-seven turns to the parts of the law that shape the marketplace: metal levels, appeals, subsidies and penalties.
